Population surveys conducted throughout its native range in western Mexico suggest that this asymptotic size is reached after several years of steady growth, with individuals rarely exceeding these dimensions even in productive lacustrine environments. The condition factor calculated from these measurements aligns well with values reported for other predatory cichlids, reinforcing the interpretation that Green guapote occupies a high trophic position in its freshwater habitats. These body size parameters serve as critical reference points for life history models and stock assessments, providing a baseline for evaluating how environmental variability influences growth trajectories across distinct populations.

Sexual maturation in Mayaheros beani occurs at a total length of 22.6 centimeters [Lp = 22.6 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 198 grams [Wwp = approximately 198 grams]. Gonadal examination of preserved specimens reveals that vitellogenesis is initiated only after females surpass this length, with the transition to reproductive readiness spanning several months as gametogenesis proceeds. The observed length at puberty also serves as an important demographic parameter, as individuals that mature earlier at smaller sizes may exhibit reduced fecundity or lower offspring survival. Field observations indicate that males tend to reach this size slightly earlier than females, a pattern common among cichlids with male-male competition for nesting sites. These size-based maturity thresholds are essential for understanding population dynamics and for setting minimum size limits in fisheries management contexts.

The spawning frequency is notably high for a cichlid of this body size, suggesting that the species compensates for moderate clutch sizes through repeated nesting events across an extended breeding season. Each clutch is deposited on a prepared substrate, typically a flat rock or excavated depression, where both parents engage in biparental care until the young reach independence. The thermal dependence of these reproductive rates is marked; preliminary experiments at lower temperatures indicate a substantial reduction in both clutch frequency and egg viability, underscoring the importance of warm-water habitats for population persistence. These findings place Green guapote among the more fecund iteroparous cichlids in its genus.

Neonatal life begins with a modest wet weight at birth of just 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], reflecting the small size of the demersal eggs from which the yolk-sac larvae emerge. Upon hatching, the prolarvae measure only a few millimeters and remain attached to the substrate via adhesive cement glands on their heads, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first several days of development. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs after approximately 5 to 7 days, at which point the larvae begin actively foraging on zooplankton and small invertebrates within the nest territory guarded by both parents. Given the tiny initial mass, the subsequent growth rate is remarkably rapid, with juveniles achieving a tenfold increase in weight within the first month under optimal thermal conditions. This high growth efficiency is characteristic of cichlids that provide extended parental care, as the energetic investment of guarding adults reduces predation risk and allows larvae to allocate more resources toward somatic growth. The small birth size also imposes constraints on early diet breadth, limiting first-feeding larvae to the smallest available prey items.

Longevity estimates for Mayaheros beani, derived from mark-recapture studies conducted at a water temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], indicate that the maximum lifespan spans approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years]. This relatively extended lifespan places Green guapote among the longer-lived cichlids in its genus, consistent with its large body size and delayed reproductive maturation. Age determination using otolith annuli confirms that individuals in natural populations regularly reach 7 to 9 years, with the oldest recorded specimen exhibiting 8 distinct annual rings. Senescence becomes apparent after the sixth year, marked by reduced growth increments, diminished gonadal output, and increased susceptibility to parasitic infections. The trade-off between prolonged lifespan and high annual fecundity highlights the species' bet-hedging strategy, where iteroparous reproduction across multiple breeding seasons buffers against stochastic environmental perturbations. Comparative analyses with sympatric cichlids suggest that the thermal regime of their native habitat, characterized by stable warm temperatures, may facilitate the maintenance of slow somatic deterioration rates throughout adult life.
